Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 47, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

[Choosing good names, because names are moulds for meanings]
(A section on the jurisprudence of this topic)

Since names are moulds for meanings and indicators of them, wisdom requires that there be a connection and correspondence between them, and that the meaning not stand toward its name as a wholly foreign thing with no relation to it. The wisdom of the Wise rejects this, and reality bears witness against it. Rather, names have an effect upon the named things, and the named things are affected by their names in goodness and ugliness, lightness and heaviness, delicacy and coarseness, as it has been said:

"Rarely have your eyes seen a bearer of a title
Except that its meaning, if you reflect on his title."

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to prefer good names, and when they sent a messenger to him he would order that he have a good name and a good face.

He would also take meanings from names, both in sleep and in waking, as when he saw in a dream that he and his companions were in the house of Uqba ibn Rafi', and they were brought dates of the Ibn Tab variety. He interpreted this as meaning that they would have elevation in this world and a good outcome in the Hereafter, and that the religion which Allah had chosen for them had ripened and become good (aṭāba). He also interpreted the ease of their affair on the Day of Hudaybiyyah from the coming of Suhayl ibn 'Amr to him.

He also urged a group to milk a sheep. A man stood up to milk it, and he said: "What is your name?" He said: "Murrah." He said: "Sit down." Another stood up, and he said: "What is your name?" He said: "I think it is Harb." He said: "Sit down." Another stood up, and he said: "What is your name?" He said: "Ya'ish." He said: "Milk it."

He also disliked places with objectionable names and disliked passing through them. On one of his campaigns he passed between two mountains, and he asked about their names. They said: "Fāḍiḥ and Mukhzin (the disgracer and the humiliating)." So he turned away from them and did not pass between them.

Since between names and the named there is the same connection, correspondence and kinship that there is between the moulds of things and their realities, and between spirits and bodies, the intellect passes from each of the two to the other. Thus Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah and others would see a person and say: "His name should be such-and-such," and they would hardly ever err. The opposite of this passing is from the name to what it names, as when 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) asked a man about his name. He said: "Jamrah (ember)." He said: "And your father's name?" He said: "Shihab (flame)." He said: "From whom?" He said: "From al-Ḥuraqah (the burning)." He said: "Where is your dwelling?" He said: "In Ḥarrat al-Nār (the fire's lava-field)." He said: "Where is your residence?" He said: "In Dhāt Laẓā (the blazing one)." He said: "Go, for your residence has been burnt." He went and found the matter was so.

So 'Umar passed from the words to their spirits and meanings, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) passed from the name Suhayl to the ease of their affair at Hudaybiyyah, and it was so. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded his community to beautify their names, and informed that they would be called by them on the Day of Resurrection. In this there is—and Allah knows best—an alert to beautifying the actions that correspond to beautifying names, so that the calling on the heads of the witnesses is by the good name and the description that suits it.

Consider how two names were derived for the Prophet (ﷺ) from his attributes that correspond to his meaning: Aḥmad and Muḥammad. He is Muḥammad because of the great number of praiseworthy qualities in him, and Aḥmad because of the nobility and excellence of those qualities over the qualities of others. Thus the name is bound to the named as the spirit is bound to the body. Likewise his (ﷺ) kunyah for Abu al-Hakam ibn Hisham was Abu Jahl, a kunyah that corresponds to his description and meaning, and he was the most deserving of creation of this kunyah. Likewise Allah's kunyah for 'Abd al-'Uzzá was Abu Lahab; since his destination was a fire of flame (lahab), this kunyah was most fitting and suitable for him, and he was most deserving and worthy of it.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah, whose name was Yathrib and was known by no other name, he changed it to Ṭaybah, because when the reproach (tathrīb) in the word Yathrib departed from it, and the goodness (ṭīb) in the meaning of Ṭaybah replaced it, it deserved this name, and was increased in goodness by it. So the goodness of its place affected its deserving of the name, and the name increased its goodness upon its goodness.

Since a good name requires its named thing and calls it near, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to one of the Arab tribes while calling them to Allah and His oneness: "O sons of 'Abd Allah, Allah has made your name and your father's name good." Observe how he called them to the servitude of Allah through the goodness of their father's name and through the meaning in it that calls to the summons. Consider also how fate required that the names of the six duellists of the Battle of Badr correspond to their conditions on that day: the disbelievers were Shaybah, 'Utbah and al-Walid, three names of weakness. Al-Walid has the beginning of weakness, and Shaybah has the end of weakness, as Allah the Exalted says: "Allah is the One who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness and grey hair" (Qur'an 30:54). And 'Utbah is from al-'Atab (reproach), so their names indicated a reproach that would befall them and a weakness that would reach them. Their counterparts among the Muslims were 'Ali, 'Ubaydah and al-Harith (may Allah be pleased with them), three names that suit their attributes: elevation, servitude, and striving, which is tillage (ḥarth). They overcame them through their servitude and their striving in the tillage of the Hereafter.

Since the name necessarily indicates its named thing and influences it, the most beloved names to Allah are those that indicate the most beloved attributes to Him, such as 'Abd Allah and 'Abd al-Rahman. The ascription of servitude to the name of Allah and the name of al-Rahman is more beloved to Him than its ascription to other names, such as al-Qahir and al-Qadir. So 'Abd al-Rahman is more beloved to Him than 'Abd al-Qadir, and 'Abd Allah is more beloved to Him than 'Abd Rabbih. This is because the bond between the servant and Allah is pure servitude, and the bond between Allah and the servant is pure mercy. By His mercy was his existence and the perfection of his existence, and the end for which He brought him into being is that he should worship Him alone in love and fear, hope and reverence and magnification, so that he is a servant of Allah. He worships Him because of what is in the name Allah of the meaning of divinity, which cannot be for anyone other than Him. And since His mercy overcame His wrath, and mercy was more beloved to Him than wrath, 'Abd al-Rahman was more beloved to Him than 'Abd al-Qahir.

[Section: On his (ﷺ) names]

All of them are descriptive epithets, not mere proper names for the sake of identification, but names derived from attributes subsisting in him that entail praise and perfection.

Among them is Muḥammad, which is the most famous of them, and by it he was named in the Torah explicitly, as we have demonstrated with clear proof in the book "Jalā' al-Afhām fī Faḍl al-Ṣalāh wa al-Salām 'alā Khayr al-Anām."

The point is that his name Muḥammad is in the Torah explicitly, in agreement with every scholar among the believing People of the Book.

Among them is Aḥmad, the name which the Messiah gave him, for a secret we mentioned in that book.

Among them: al-Mutawakkil (the one who relies), al-Mahi (the eraser), al-Hashir (the gatherer), al-'Aqib (the last), al-Muqaffi (the one who follows), Nabi al-Tawbah (the Prophet of repentance), Nabi al-Rahmah (the Prophet of mercy), Nabi al-Malhamah (the Prophet of the great battle), al-Fatih (the opener), and al-Amin (the trustworthy).

Joined to these names are: al-Shahid (the witness), al-Mubashshir (the bringer of good news), al-Bashir (the bearer of good news), al-Nadhir (the warner), al-Qasim (the distributor), al-Dahuk (the one who laughs), al-Qattal (the slayer), 'Abd Allah (the servant of Allah), al-Siraj al-Munir (the shining lamp), Sayyid Walad Adam (the master of the sons of Adam), Sahib Liwa' al-Hamd (the bearer of the banner of praise), Sahib al-Maqam al-Mahmud (the possessor of the praised station), and other names; for if his names are attributes of praise, then for every attribute he has a name. But one must distinguish between an attribute specific to him or predominant in him from which a name is derived for him, and an attribute shared with others from which there is no name specific to him.

Jubayr ibn Mut'im said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named himself for us with names, and said: 'I am Muhammad, and I am Ahmad, and I am al-Mahi, through whom Allah erases disbelief; and I am al-Hashir, at whose feet people will be gathered; and al-'Aqib, after whom there is no prophet.'"

His (ﷺ) names are of two kinds:

The first is specific to him, which no other messenger shares with him, such as Muhammad, Ahmad, al-'Aqib, al-Hashir, al-Muqaffi, and Nabi al-Malhamah.

The second is that which another messenger shares with him in its meaning, but he has its perfection from it; so he is specific in its perfection, not in its root, such as Rasul Allah (Messenger of Allah), Nabi (Prophet), 'Abd (servant), al-Shahid, al-Mubashshir, al-Nadhir, Nabi al-Rahmah, and Nabi al-Tawbah.

As for if there were made for him from each of his attributes a name, his names would exceed two hundred, such as al-Sadiq (the truthful), al-MasdUq (the one believed), al-Ra'uf al-Rahim (the kind and merciful), and the like.

On this, some people have said: "Allah has a thousand names, and the Prophet (ﷺ) has a thousand names," as said by Abu al-Khattab ibn Dihyah, and his intention was the attributes.

[Section: On explaining the meanings of his (ﷺ) names]

As for Muḥammad, it is a passive participle (ism maf'ul) from ḥamida, so he is Muḥammad when he has many of the qualities for which he is praised; and for this reason it is more emphatic than maḥmud, for maḥmud is from the unaugmented triliteral, while Muḥammad is from the doubled form for intensification. He is the one who is praised more than other human beings are praised. For this reason, and Allah knows best, he was named by it in the Torah, because of the many praiseworthy qualities by which he, his religion and his community are described in the Torah, to the extent that Musa (peace be upon him) wished to be among them. We have dealt with this meaning, with its evidences, in that place, and we explained the error of Abu al-Qasim al-Suhayli in making the matter the reverse, and claiming that his name in the Torah is Ahmad.

As for Aḥmad, it is a name on the pattern of the comparative (af'al al-tafdil), also derived from ḥamd. People have differed concerning it: is it in the sense of an active participle or a passive one? A group said: it is in the sense of the active participle, meaning that his praise of Allah is greater than others' praise of Him, so its meaning is "the most praising of those who praise their Lord." They preferred this view on the grounds that the pattern of the comparative is to be formed from the verb of the doer, not from a verb that falls upon the object. They said: for this reason one does not say "mā aḍrab Zaydan" (how much he strikes Zayd!) nor "Zayd adrab min 'Amr" in regard to the striking that falls upon him, nor "mā ashrabahu lil-mā'" and "ākaluhu lil-khubz" and the like.

They said: because the comparative and the exclamatory form (fi'l al-ta'ajjub) are formed only from the intransitive verb. For this reason their transfer is assumed from fa'ala and fa'ila (with open and with kasra in the middle) to fa'ula (with damma in the middle). They said: for this reason it is made transitive to the object by the hamza, so its hamza is for transitivity, as in your saying "mā aẓraf Zaydan" (how witty Zayd is!) and "akram 'Amran" (how generous 'Amr is!), and their origin is from ẓaruf and karum. They said: because the one about whom the exclamation is made is the doer in origin, so its verb must be non-transitive. They said: as for the like of "mā aḍrab Zaydan li-'Amr," it is transferred from fa'ala (with open middle) to fa'ula (with damma in the middle), then made transitive in that state by the hamza. They said: the proof of this is their bringing the lam, so they say "mā aḍrab Zaydan li-'Amr," and had it remained transitive, it would have been said "mā aḍrab Zaydan 'Amran," because it is transitive to one object by itself and to the other by the transitivity hamza. So when they made it transitive to the object by the transitivity hamza, they made it transitive to the other by the lam. This is what caused them to say that they are formed only from the verb of the doer, not from the verb that falls upon the object.

Others disputed this with them and said: it is permissible to form them both from the verb of the doer and from the verb that falls upon the object, and the abundance of hearing of this is the clearest evidence of its permissibility. The Arabs say: "mā ashghalahu bi-l-shay'" (how occupied with the thing he is!), and it is from shughila, so he is mashghul; and likewise they say "mā awla'ahu bi-kadhā" (how fond of such-and-such he is!), and it is from ūlia bi-l-shay', so he is mūlaʿ bihi, passive only; and likewise their saying "mā a'jabahu bi-kadhā," which is from ujiba bihi. They say "mā aḥabbahu ilayya," which is an exclamation from the verb of the object, and his being beloved to you. And likewise: "mā abghaḍahu ilayya" and "amqatahu ilayya."

There is here a well-known question that Sibawayh mentioned: you say "mā abghaḍanī lahu," "mā aḥabbanī lahu," and "mā amqatanī lahu" when you are the hater who dislikes and the lover who loathes, so you are exclaiming at the act of the doer. And you say "mā abghaḍanī ilayhi," "mā amqatanī ilayhi," and "mā aḥabbanī ilayhi" when you are the one hated, loathed, or loved, so you are exclaiming at the act that falls upon the object. So what is with the lam is for the doer, and what is with "ilā" is for the object.

Most grammarians do not give this as a reason, but what is said about its cause, and God knows best, is this: the lam (al-lam, the particle "to/for") is, in meaning, for the doer (al-fa'il), as in your saying: "For whom is this?" and one answers: "For Zayd," so the lam is brought. As for ila ("to"), it is, in meaning, for the object (al-maf'ul), so you say: "To whom does this book reach?" and one answers: "To Abd Allah." The secret of this is that the lam originally denotes ownership and exclusivity, and entitlement belongs only to the doer who owns and deserves; while ila denotes the limit of an end, and the end is the terminus of what the verb requires, so it is more fitting for the object, since it completes what the verb demands. And among the expressions of wonder at the act of the object is the words of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr about the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Indeed, he is more frightening to me when I speak to him, and it is said that you are imprisoned and slain,
Of a lion-cub among the lions of the lions, whose dwelling is in the valley of Athar, a thicket before him is another thicket."

Here "akhwaf" (more frightening) is from "khuwwifa," so he is "makhuf" (one who is feared), not from "khafa." Likewise the saying "ma ajanna Zayd!" (how mad Zayd is!) is from "junna," so he is "majnun" (mad). This is the view of the Kufans and those who agree with them.

The Basrans said: All of this is anomalous (shadhdh) and is not to be relied upon, so we do not disturb the rules with it, and one must confine oneself to what is heard. The Kufans said: The frequency of this in their speech, both in prose and in verse, prevents treating it as anomalous, because the anomalous is what contradicts their usage and regular speech, and this does not contradict that. They said: As for your assumption that the verb is intransitive and is transferred to the pattern fa'ula, it is an arbitrary claim with no proof. And what you rely upon regarding transitivity by the hamza and so on, the matter is not as you think; the hamza in this form is not for transitivity, but only to indicate the meaning of wonder and preference, like the alif of fa'il, the mim of maf'ul, the waw and ta' of ifti'al and muta'awa'a, and similar additions that attach to the triliteral verb to show the addition beyond its bare form. This is the reason that brings this hamza, not the transitivity of the verb.

They said: What indicates this is that the verb which is made transitive by the hamza may also be made transitive by a preposition or by doubling, as in: "jalastu bihi" and "ajlastuhu," "qumtu bihi" and "aqamtuhu," and their like; and here nothing other than the hamza can take its place. It is thus known that it is not for bare transitivity either, since it combines with the transitive ba', as in: "akrim bihi" and "ahsin bihi," and two transitivities are not combined on one verb.

Also, they say: "ma a'taahu lil-darahim" (how he gives to the dirhams!) and "aksaahu lil-thiyab" (how he clothes for the garments!), and this is from the transitive "a'ta" and "kasa." It is not valid to suppose it is transferred from "ata" (to take), for when the hamza of transitivity is added to it, the meaning is corrupted, since the wonder arises from his giving, not from his taking, which is "ata" (to take). The hamza in it is the hamza of wonder and preference, and the hamza of its verb has been deleted, so it cannot be said that it is for transitivity.

They said: As for your statement that it is transitive by the lam in such as "ma adraba-hu li-Zayd..." to the end, bringing the lam here is not for what you mentioned of the necessity of the verb, but it is brought to strengthen it when it has weakened by being prevented from full inflection and being bound to one fixed form, which takes it out of the usual patterns of verbs, so it is weakened in its governing and action, and so it is strengthened by the lam, just as it is strengthened by it when its complement precedes it, and when it is a derivative. This view is the preferred one, as you see.

Let us return to the purpose and say: the form "Ahmad" according to the first opinion means "the most praising of people to his Lord," and according to these means "the most deserving and most fitting of people to be praised," so it is like "Muhammad" in meaning, except that the difference between them is that "Muhammad" is one who has many praiseworthy qualities, while "Ahmad" is one who is praised more excellently than others are praised. Thus "Muhammad" concerns quantity and multiplicity, and "Ahmad" concerns quality and manner, so he deserves more praise than others deserve and a more excellent praise than others deserve, and so he is praised with the greatest praise and the most excellent praise that mankind has ever offered. Both names then denote the object (the one praised), and this is more eloquent in praising him and more complete in meaning. Had the meaning of the doer been intended, he would be called "al-Hammad," that is, one who praises much, for he (ﷺ) was the most praising of creation to his Lord; so if his name Ahmad were based on his praise of his Lord, the more suitable would have been "al-Hammad," just as his community was named by that.

Also: these two names were derived from his good character and praiseworthy distinctions, for which he deserved to be named Muhammad (ﷺ); and Ahmad is the one whom the people of the heavens, the people of the earth, the people of this world and the people of the Hereafter praise, because of the abundance of his praiseworthy qualities, which exceed the count of those who count and the enumeration of those who enumerate. We have elaborated this meaning in the book on prayer and peace upon him (ﷺ). We have mentioned here only a few words, as required by the state of the traveler, the scattering of his heart and the dispersion of his resolve. And from God is help, and upon Him is reliance.

As for his name al-Mutawakkil (the one who relies upon God), in Sahih al-Bukhari, on the authority of Abd Allah ibn Amr, who said: "I read in the Torah the description of the Prophet (ﷺ): Muhammad, the Messenger of God, My servant and My messenger; I have named him al-Mutawakkil; he is neither harsh nor coarse, nor does he shout in the markets, nor does he repay evil with evil, but he pardons and overlooks; and I will not take him until I have set straight through him the crooked community, by their saying: There is no god but God."

He (ﷺ) is most deserving of this name, because he relied upon God in establishing the religion with a reliance in which no one shared with him.

As for al-Maahi (the Eraser), al-Hashir (the Gatherer), al-Muqaffi (the Successor), and al-Aqib (the Last), they have been explained in the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im. Al-Maahi is the one through whom God erased disbelief, and no one of creation had disbelief erased by him as much as was erased through the Prophet (ﷺ), for he was sent when all the people of the earth were disbelievers, except remnants of the People of the Book, who were between idol-worshippers, Jews who earned anger, Christians who went astray, Sabians of the dahri type who knew no Lord and no return, and worshippers of the stars, worshippers of fire, and philosophers who knew not the laws of the prophets and did not affirm them. God, glorified is He, through His Messenger erased all that until the religion of God prevailed over every religion, and his religion reached as far as the night and day reach, and his call traveled like the sun across the regions.

As for al-Hashir, gathering (hashr) is joining and assembling, so he is the one upon whose footsteps people will be gathered, as if he was sent so that people would be gathered.

Al-Aqib is the one who came after the prophets, so there is no prophet after him, for the aqib is the last, and he is like the seal; for this reason he was called al-Aqib without qualification, meaning: he came after the prophets, following their footsteps.

As for al-Muqaffi, it is similar: he is the one who followed upon the traces of those who preceded him, so God made him follow upon the traces of those who came before him among the messengers; and this word is derived from qafw, one says: "qafahu yaqfuhu" when he lags behind him, and from it: qafiyat al-ra's (the back of the head) and qafiyat al-bayt (the rhyme of the verse). So al-Muqaffi is the one who followed those before him among the messengers, and so he was their seal and their last.

As for the Prophet of Repentance: he is the one through whom God opened the gate of repentance to the people of the earth, and God accepted their repentance with a repentance that the people of the earth had not obtained like before him. The Prophet (ﷺ) was the most frequent of people in seeking forgiveness and repentance, to the extent that they counted for him in a single sitting one hundred times: "My Lord, forgive me and accept my repentance, indeed You are the Ever-Relenting, the Oft-Forgiving."

He used to say: "O people, repent to God your Lord, for I repent to God a hundred times a day." Likewise the repentance of his community is more complete than that of all other nations, quicker in acceptance and easier in obtaining, whereas the repentance of those before them was among the hardest things; to the extent that the repentance of the Children of Israel from worshipping the calf was the killing of themselves. As for this community, because of its honour before God, the Exalted, He made its repentance regret and abandonment (of sin).

As for the Prophet of the Great Battle (malhama): he is the one sent to fight the enemies of God. No prophet and his community ever fought as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his community fought, and the great battles that occurred and occur between his community and the disbelievers have no precedent like them before him, for his community kills the disbelievers in the regions of the earth across the successive ages, and they have inflicted upon them battles that no other community has done.

As for the Prophet of Mercy: he is the one whom God sent as a mercy to the worlds, so all the people of the earth were shown mercy through him, believers and disbelievers alike. As for the believers, they obtained the fullest share of mercy. As for the disbelievers, the People of the Book among them lived under his shade, beneath his rope and his covenant; and as for those among them who killed him and his community, they hastened them to the Fire and relieved him from the long life, which increases him only in severity of punishment in the Hereafter.

As for al-Fatih (the Opener): he is the one through whom God opened the gate of guidance after it had been closed, and opened through him blind eyes, deaf ears and veiled hearts; God opened through him the cities of the disbelievers, opened through him the gates of Paradise, and opened through him the paths of beneficial knowledge and righteous action; so through him He opened this world and the Hereafter, the hearts, the hearing, the sights and the cities.

As for al-Amin (the Trustworthy): he is the most worthy of all the worlds of this name; he is the trustee of God over His revelation and His religion, and he is the trustee of those in the heavens and the trustee of those on the earth. For this reason they called him al-Amin before prophethood.

As for al-Dahuk al-Qattal (the Smiling, the Fighter): these are two paired names that are not separated from one another. He is smiling to the faces of the believers, not frowning, nor scowling, nor angry, nor harsh; and he is a fighter against the enemies of God, not taking in regard to them the blame of any blamer.

As for al-Bashir (the Bringer of Glad Tidings): he is the one who gives good news of reward to whoever obeys him, and the warner (al-nadhir), who warns whoever disobeys him of punishment. God has called him His servant in several places of His Book, among them His saying: ﴿And when the servant of God stood up calling upon Him﴾ [al-Jinn: 19] and His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan: 1]

and His saying: ﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10] and His saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23]

And it is established from him in the Sahih that he said: "I am the master of the children of Adam on the Day of Resurrection, and I say it without boasting." God named him a illuminating lamp (siraj munir), and named the sun a blazing lamp (siraj wahhaj).

Al-Munir (the Illuminating) is the one who gives light without burning, unlike al-Wahhaj, for in it there is a kind of burning and blazing.

**(On the Wisdom and Secrets of Trial)**

Know that the creation of those who disbelieve in Him, associate others with Him, and oppose Him brings about splendid wisdoms and manifest signs that would not otherwise occur. Had the people of Noah not disbelieved, the sign of the Flood would not have appeared, and people would not still be speaking of it across the ages. Had 'Ad not disbelieved, the sign of the barren wind (al-rih al-'aqim), which destroyed everything it passed over, would not have appeared. Had the people of Salih not disbelieved, the sign of their destruction by the Blast (al-sayhah) would not have appeared. And had Pharaoh not disbelieved, those signs and marvels, which nations recount one after another, would not have appeared. Through them, whoever God willed was guided, and whoever perished, perished after clear proof, and whoever lived, lived after clear proof. Through them, God's grace, justice, and wisdom became manifest, as did the signs of His messengers and their truthfulness. Thus, the opposition of the messengers, the breaking and refuting of their proofs, the answering of such opposition, and God's destruction of their opponents are among the greatest evidences of their truthfulness and its clearest demonstrations.

Likewise, had the polytheists not come at Badr with their armor, iron, numbers, and might, that great sign would not have occurred, along with the faith, guidance, and good that resulted from it and that would not have existed without it. We have already explained that what depends upon a thing does not exist without it, and that the existence of what necessitates something without what it necessitates is impossible. How much the story of Badr has enriched a corner that had become inhabited by faith! How many doors were opened by it to those of understanding, through which they reached guidance and certainty! How many were thereby made beloved to the All-Merciful and a source of vexation to Satan! The corruption that occurred in its midst for the disbelievers is utterly submerged in comparison with its benefits and wisdoms. It is like the harm of rain when it cuts off a traveler, soaks garments, and damages some houses, compared with the benefit to the general public. Consider what the Flood and the drowning of Pharaoh's household brought to the nations in guidance and faith, which overwhelmed the corruption of those who perished in it, so that it vanished in the face of its benefit and wisdom. How many wisdoms God has in His signs, by which He tested His enemies and honored His allies, and how many signs, proofs, insights, and reminders He has in them!

For this reason, He (glorified is He) commanded His Messenger to remind his community through them, saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We indeed sent Moses with Our signs, [saying]: Bring your people out of darkness into light, and remind them of the days of God. Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one. And [mention] when Moses said to his people: Remember God's blessing upon you, when He saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted on you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women; and in that was a great trial from your Lord.﴾

So he reminded them of His days and His favors, and of their deliverance from their enemy and his destruction while they watched. Thereby there came about, through that remembrance, gratitude, love, glorification, and reverence of Him, such that the corruption of the slaughter and killing of the sons was dissolved and vanished, for they came to bliss and were freed from the corruption of servitude to Pharaoh.

**(Chapter)**

God (glorified is He) has mentioned in more than one place in His Book that a second good may be a reward for a first good, and that a sin may be a punishment for an earlier sin. The first is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if they had done what they were admonished to do, it would have been better for them and firmer in steadfastness. And We would have given them from Us a great reward, and We would have guided them to a straight path.﴾ And He said: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths.﴾ And He said: ﴿By it God guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace, and brings them out of darkness into light by His permission, and guides them to a straight path.﴾

As for His saying: ﴿And those who were killed in the way of God, He will not let their deeds go astray. He will guide them and set their minds right.﴾

It is possible that this is not of that kind, and that the guidance is to the path of Paradise in the Hereafter, since He attached this reward to their being killed.

And it is possible that it is of that kind, and that His saying ﴿He will guide them and set their minds right﴾ is information from Him, (glorified is He), about what He does with those who were killed in His way before they were killed.

He expressed it in the future tense to inform that He renews for them, at every moment, a type of guidance and the setting right of their minds, one after another.

If you say, how can that future tense be a report about those who were killed?

I say: the predicate is His saying ﴿He will not let their deeds go astray﴾, meaning that He does not nullify them for them or deprive them of them. This is after they were killed. The listener therefore returns each sentence to its proper time, since the meaning is clear and not ambiguous. This is frequent in the Qur'an, and God knows best.

**(Chapter)**

The fourth stage of guidance is guidance to Paradise and Hell on the Day of Resurrection. God the Exalted said: ﴿Gather those who did wrong, their companions, and what they used to worship besides God, and lead them to the path of the Blazing Fire.﴾

And He the Exalted said: ﴿And those who were killed in the way of God, He will not let their deeds go astray. He will guide them and set their minds right.﴾

This is guidance after their killing.

It was said: the meaning is that He will guide them to the path of Paradise and set their condition right in the Hereafter by pleasing their adversaries and accepting their deeds.

Ibn 'Abbas said: He will guide them to the most rightly guided affairs and will protect them during their lifetime in this world.

This view was found problematic, because it reports about those killed in His way that He "will guide them."

Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) chose it and said: "He sets their minds right in livelihood and the rulings of this world."

He said: "He intends by it that He gathers for them the good of this world and the Hereafter."

According to this view, the phrase ﴿who were killed in the way of God﴾ must be understood in a sense that allows affirming guidance and the setting right of their minds.

**(Section: On their knowledge of their stations and dwellings when they enter Paradise, even if they had not seen them before)**

God the Exalted said: ﴿And those who were killed in the way of God, He will not let their deeds go astray. He will guide them, set their minds right, and admit them into Paradise, which He has made known to them.﴾

Mujahid said: "Its people are guided to their houses and dwellings without error, as though they had lived in them since they were created, without asking anyone for directions to them."

Ibn 'Abbas, in the transmission of Abu Salih, said: "They know their stations better than the people of Paradise do when they return to their dwellings."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "They recognize it as you recognize your houses in this world when you return from Friday prayer." This is the view of the majority of the commentators, and a summary of their views is what Abu 'Ubaydah said: "'Arrafa lahum" means he made it clear to them, so that they recognized it without deduction.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "It has reached us that the angel assigned to guard the children of Adam walks in Paradise, and the son of Adam follows him until he reaches the farthest dwelling that is his. He then recognizes everything God gave him in Paradise. When he enters his dwelling and his wives, the angel departs from him."

Salamah ibn Kuhayl said: "He made its paths known to them," meaning that He made them known to them so that they could find their way to it.

Al-Hasan said: "God described Paradise to them in this world, so when they enter it they recognize it by its description."

According to this view, the making known took place in this world, and the meaning is: He admits them into the Paradise which He made known to them.

According to the first view, the making known takes place in the Hereafter.

All of this applies if it is said that it derives from "ta'rif" (making known).

There is another view that it derives from "'arf," which means a pleasant fragrance. This is the choice of al-Zajjaj, meaning its fragrance, and from it comes the expression "ta'am mu'arraf," meaning perfumed food.

It was also said that it derives from "'arf," which means succession, meaning that its good things and delights follow them one after another.

The first view is the correct one: He (glorified is He) made it known to them and explained it in a way by which each person knows his abode and dwelling, so that he does not go beyond it to another.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Qatadah, from Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said:

"When the believers are delivered from the Fire, they are held back on a bridge between Paradise and the Fire, and they settle the wrongs that they committed against one another in the world. When they have been purified and cleansed, they are permitted to enter Paradise. By Him in whose hand my soul is, one of them will know his dwelling in Paradise better than he knows his home in the world."

In another Musnad, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "By Him who sent me with the truth, you are not more knowledgeable in this world about your own conditions and dwellings than the people of Paradise are about their conditions, their wives, and their dwellings when they enter Paradise."

**(On the Wisdom and Secrets of Trial)**

Know that the creation of those who disbelieve in Him, associate others with Him, and oppose Him brings about splendid wisdoms and manifest signs that would not otherwise occur. Had the people of Noah not disbelieved, the sign of the Flood would not have appeared, and people would not still be speaking of it across the ages. Had 'Ad not disbelieved, the sign of the barren wind (al-rih al-'aqim), which destroyed everything it passed over, would not have appeared. Had the people of Salih not disbelieved, the sign of their destruction by the Blast (al-sayhah) would not have appeared. And had Pharaoh not disbelieved, those signs and marvels, which nations recount one after another, would not have appeared. Through them, whoever God willed was guided, and whoever perished, perished after clear proof, and whoever lived, lived after clear proof. Through them, God's grace, justice, and wisdom became manifest, as did the signs of His messengers and their truthfulness. Thus, the opposition of the messengers, the breaking and refuting of their proofs, the answering of such opposition, and God's destruction of their opponents are among the greatest evidences of their truthfulness and its clearest demonstrations.

Likewise, had the polytheists not come at Badr with their armor, iron, numbers, and might, that great sign would not have occurred, along with the faith, guidance, and good that resulted from it and that would not have existed without it. We have already explained that what depends upon a thing does not exist without it, and that the existence of what necessitates something without what it necessitates is impossible. How much the story of Badr has enriched a corner that had become inhabited by faith! How many doors were opened by it to those of understanding, through which they reached guidance and certainty! How many were thereby made beloved to the All-Merciful and a source of vexation to Satan! The corruption that occurred in its midst for the disbelievers is utterly submerged in comparison with its benefits and wisdoms. It is like the harm of rain when it cuts off a traveler, soaks garments, and damages some houses, compared with the benefit to the general public. Consider what the Flood and the drowning of Pharaoh's household brought to the nations in guidance and faith, which overwhelmed the corruption of those who perished in it, so that it vanished in the face of its benefit and wisdom. How many wisdoms God has in His signs, by which He tested His enemies and honored His allies, and how many signs, proofs, insights, and reminders He has in them!

For this reason, He (glorified is He) commanded His Messenger to remind his community through them, saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We indeed sent Moses with Our signs, [saying]: Bring your people out of darkness into light, and remind them of the days of God. Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one. And [mention] when Moses said to his people: Remember God's blessing upon you, when He saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted on you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women; and in that was a great trial from your Lord.﴾

Al-Tabarani said: Mu'adh ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, who said: Ali ibn al-Madini narrated to us, who said: Rayhan ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Ubada ibn Mansur, from Ayyub, from Abu Qilaba, from Isma'il, from Thawban ibn Thawban, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

"When a man plucks a fruit from Paradise, another grows in its place."

And Abdullah ibn al-Imam Ahmad said: Uqba ibn Mukram al-Ammi narrated to me, who said: Rab'i ibn Ibrahim ibn Ulayya narrated to us, from Awf, from Qassama ibn Zuhayr, from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

"Allah sent Adam down from Paradise, peace be upon him, and taught him the craft of everything and provided him with fruits of Paradise. Your fruits here are from the fruits of Paradise, except that they change, whereas those do not change." And it has already been mentioned that the fruit of the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha) is like large jars.

In Sahih Muslim, from the narration of Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said:

"Paradise was displayed to me, to the extent that if I had taken a cluster from it, I would have taken it." And in another wording: "I reached out and took a cluster from it, but my hand fell short of it."

Abu Khaythama said: Abdullah ibn Ja'far narrated to us, who said: Ubaydullah narrated to us, who said: Ibn Aqil narrated to us, from Jabir, who said: "While we were praying the noon prayer, the Messenger of Allah stepped forward, so we stepped forward with him. Then he reached out to take something, then he drew back. When he finished the prayer, Ubayy ibn Ka'b said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, you did something in your prayer today that you had never done before.' He said:

'Paradise was displayed to me, with its brightness and radiance. I reached out and took a cluster of grapes to bring to you, but it was kept from me. Had I brought it to you, you would have eaten from it from between the heaven and the earth, and it would not have diminished.'"

Ibn al-Mubarak said: Sufyan informed us, from Hammad, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said:

"The fruit of Paradise is like large jars and buckets, whiter than milk, sweeter than honey, softer than butter, and it has no pit."

Sa'id ibn Mansur said: Shurayk narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara' ibn Azib, who said: "The people of Paradise eat from the fruits of Paradise standing, sitting and reclining, in whatever state they wish."

**(Section: On the mention of the rivers of Paradise, its springs, their kinds, and the course along which they flow)**

The verse of Allah, the Exalted, has been repeated in the Qur'an in several places: ﴿Rivers flow beneath them﴾, and in one place: ﴿Rivers flow beneath it﴾, and in another place: ﴿Rivers flow beneath them﴾ [the wording differs slightly in each].

This indicates several matters:

First: that the rivers in it exist in reality.

Second: that they are flowing rivers, not stagnant ones.

Third: that they run beneath their upper chambers, palaces and gardens, as is familiar with the rivers of this world. Some exegetes have thought that the meaning of this is that they flow by their command and direction, as they wish. What led them to this is that when they heard that its rivers flow without a trench, flowing over the surface of the earth, they took the phrase "flow beneath them" to mean that they flow by their command, since what is above a place cannot be beneath it. These people have been afflicted by weakness of understanding. Even though the rivers of Paradise flow without a trench, they are beneath the palaces, dwellings and chambers, and beneath the trees. He, glory be to Him, did not say "beneath its ground." He has informed us of the flowing of rivers beneath people in this world, saying: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established on the earth as We have not established you, and We sent down the sky upon them in abundant rain, and made rivers flow beneath them?﴾ This is according to what is familiar and customary. Likewise is what He related of Pharaoh's words: ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾. And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿In both of them are two gushing springs﴾.

Ibn Abi Shayba said: Yahya ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Ashab, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, who said: "Two gushing springs of water and fruits." And Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Aban, from Anas, who said: "Two gushing springs of musk and ambergris, gushing over the dwellings of the people of Paradise as rain gushes over the dwellings of the people of this world." And Abdullah ibn Idris narrated to us, from his father, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', who said: "The two that flow are better than the two that gush."

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿The description of the Garden which the righteous are promised: in it are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of purified honey, and for them therein is every kind of fruit, and forgiveness from their Lord﴾.

He, glory be to Him, mentioned these four kinds and negated from each of them the defect that affects it in this world. The defect of water is that it becomes foul and stagnant from long standing. The defect of milk is that its taste changes to sourness and it becomes sharp. The defect of wine is the disliked taste that is contrary to pleasure in drinking it. The defect of honey is that it is not purified.

This is among the signs of the Lord, exalted, that rivers should flow from kinds that habit has not caused to flow in this world, flowing without a trench, and that He negates from them the defects which prevent the perfection of pleasure in them, just as He negates from the wine of Paradise all the defects of the wine of this world: headache, intoxication that corrupts the mind (ghawl), depletion (infad), and lack of pleasure. These are five defects of the wine of this world: it destroys the mind, and much idle talk accompanies its drinking, indeed its drinkers find delight in it only through idle talk; it depletes the self and depletes wealth; it splits the head; its taste is disgusting; it is an abomination from the work of Satan; it casts enmity and hatred among people; it turns people away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer; it calls to fornication, and perhaps calls to committing sin with a daughter, a sister, and close female relatives; it removes jealousy; it brings shame, regret and disgrace; it links its drinker to the most deficient kind of human beings, namely the insane; it strips him of the best names and characteristics and clothes him with the worst names and attributes; it facilitates killing a soul and divulging a secret, the divulging of which harms or destroys him; it brings him into fellowship with the devils in squandering wealth which Allah made a means of sustenance for him and did not oblige him to spend upon; it tears down veils, reveals secrets, points to shameful things, makes the commission of ugly and sinful acts easy, and removes the reverence for what is forbidden from the heart. Its addict is like a worshipper of an idol. How many wars has it stirred up, how much wealth has it impoverished, how many honourable people has it humiliated, how many nobles has it debased, how much blessing has it removed, how much retribution has it brought, how much affection has it dissolved, how much enmity has it woven, and how many a man and his wife has it separated, taking away his heart and departing with his mind! How much sorrow has it caused, how many tears has it drawn! How many doors of good has it closed in the face of its drinker, and how many doors of evil has it opened for him! How many calamities has it brought about, and how quickly has it hastened his death! How much disgrace has it caused, and how much love has it drawn upon its drinker, and how much baseness has it drawn upon him! It is the sum of sin, the key to evil, the robber of blessings, and the bringer of retribution. And if there were no vice in it except that it does not combine with the wine of Paradise in the belly of a servant, as has been established from him, peace be upon him, that he said:

"Whoever drinks wine in this world will not drink it in the Hereafter."

That would suffice. The defects of wine are many times more than what we have mentioned, and all of them are negated from the wine of Paradise.

If it is said: Allah, the Exalted, has described the rivers as flowing, and it is known that flowing water does not become foul, so what is the benefit of His saying ﴿unaltered﴾?

It is answered: Flowing water, although it does not become foul, if some of it is taken and it stays a long time, it becomes foul. But the water of Paradise is not subject to this, even if it remains for however long.

Reflect on the combination of these four rivers, which are the finest drinks of people. This one is for their drinking and purification; this one is for their sustenance and nourishment; this one is for their delight and joy; and this one is for their intercession and benefit. And Allah knows best.

**(Section)**

The rivers of Paradise burst forth from its highest point, then descend, flowing downward to the lowest of its levels. This is as al-Bukhari related in his Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said:

"Indeed, in Paradise there are one hundred levels, which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, prepared for those who strive in His cause; between each two levels is as the distance between the heaven and the earth. So when you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the middle of Paradise and its highest part, and above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful, and from it the rivers of Paradise burst forth."

And al-Tirmidhi related something similar from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ubada ibn al-Samit, and the wording of the hadith of Ubada is:

"Paradise has one hundred levels; between each two levels is a distance of one hundred years. Al-Firdaws is its highest level, and from it are the four rivers, and the Throne is above it. So when you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws al-A'la (the highest Firdaws)."

In al-Mu'jam of al-Tabarani, from the hadith of al-Hasan, from Samura, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

"Al-Firdaws is the elevated ground of Paradise, its highest and its middle, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth."

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Shu'ba, from Qatada, who said: Anas ibn Malik informed me that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

"I was raised to the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary in the seventh heaven, its fruit like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves like the ears of elephants. From its base there emerge two apparent rivers and two hidden rivers. I said: 'O Jibril, what is this?' He said: 'As for the two hidden rivers, they are in Paradise; as for the two apparent ones, they are the Nile and the Euphrates.'"

And in his Sahih also, from the hadith of Hammam, from Qatada, from Anas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

"While I was walking in Paradise, suddenly there was a river whose two banks were domes of pearls and hollow pearls. I said: 'What is this, O Jibril?' He said: 'This is al-Kawthar which your Lord has given you.' Then the angel struck with his hand, and behold, it was a clay of musk, pungent."

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of al-Mukhtar ibn Falful, from Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Al-Kawthar is a river in Paradise which my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, promised me."

Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Ansari said: Humayd al-Tawil narrated to us, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

"I entered Paradise, and behold, there was a river flowing, whose two banks were tents of pearls. I struck my hand into what was flowing in it, the water, and behold, it was pungent musk. I said: 'To whom does this belong, O Jibril?' He said: 'This is al-Kawthar which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has given you.'"

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of al-Jurayri, from Hakim ibn Mu'awiya, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said:

"Indeed, in Paradise there is a sea of water, a sea of honey, a sea of milk, and a sea of wine, and then the rivers split off after that."

He said: This is a hasan sahih hadith.

Al-Hakim said: Al-Asamm narrated to us, who said: al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman narrated to us, who said: Asad ibn Musa narrated to us, who said: Ibn Thawban narrated to us, from Ata' ibn Qurra, from Abdullah ibn Samura, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

"Whoever wishes that Allah gives him wine to drink in the Hereafter, let him abandon it in this world; and whoever wishes that Allah clothes him in silk in the Hereafter, let him abandon it in this world. The rivers of Paradise gush forth from beneath hills or beneath mountains of musk. And if the lowest of the people of Paradise had an adornment equal to the adornment of all the people of this world combined, what Allah adorns him with in the Hereafter would be better than the adornment of all the people of this world."

And al-A'mash mentioned, from Amr ibn Murra, from Masruq, from Abdullah, who said:

"Indeed, the rivers of Paradise gush forth from a mountain of musk."

This is a sound mawquf report (a report ending with a Companion).

al-Sha'bi said: "Whoever wishes to take the most reliable position in judgment, let him take the saying of Umar."

Some of the Successors (tabi'un) said: "I went to Umar, and the jurists in his presence were like children; he surpassed them in his jurisprudence (fiqh) and his knowledge." [Section: Uthman ibn Affan]

Uthman ibn Affan was also among those who issued fatwas. Ibn Jarir said: "However, he had no well-known companions, and those who transmitted from Umar his fatwas, his legal positions, and his rulings in the religion after him were more numerous than those who transmitted and conveyed from Uthman."

Ibn Mas'ud said: "If Ibn Abbas had reached our age, no man among us would have been able to match him."

Makhul said: "It was said to Ibn Abbas, 'How did you obtain this knowledge?'" He said: "With an inquiring tongue and an understanding heart."

Mujahid said: "Ibn Abbas was called 'the sea' because of the abundance of his knowledge."

Tawus said: "I met about fifty of the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. When Ibn Abbas mentioned something and they disagreed with him, he would not stop until he had established it for them." It was said to Tawus, "You met the companions of Muhammad ﷺ and then attached yourself to Ibn Abbas?" He said: "I met seventy of the companions of Muhammad ﷺ. When they disputed over something, they would end up at the saying of Ibn Abbas."

Ibn Abi Najih said: "The companions of Ibn Abbas used to say: 'Ibn Abbas is more knowledgeable than Umar, than Ali, and than Abdullah.' They would mention people, and the people would attack them, so they would say: 'Do not rush against us. None of these men had knowledge except that he had something that his companion did not have, but Ibn Abbas had gathered all of it.'"

al-A'mash said: "When you saw Ibn Abbas, you would say, 'He is the most handsome of people.' When he spoke, you would say, 'He is the most eloquent of people.' When he related hadith, you would say, 'He is the most knowledgeable of people.'"

Mujahid said: "When Ibn Abbas explained something, you could see light upon him."

[Section: Umar ibn al-Khattab]

al-Sha'bi said: "Whoever wishes to take the most reliable position in judgment, let him take the saying of Umar."

Mujahid said: "When people differ over something, look at what Umar did and take it."

Ibn al-Musayyib said: "I know of no one after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ more knowledgeable than Umar ibn al-Khattab." He also said: "Abdullah used to say: 'If people took one valley and one path, and Umar took a valley and a path, I would take the valley and path of Umar.'"

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on surah 47, verses 16–17 (part 2 of 2):

Some of the Successors (tabi'un) said: "I went to Umar, and the jurists in his presence were like children; he surpassed them in his jurisprudence (fiqh) and his knowledge." Muhammad ibn Jarir said: "No one had well-known companions who recorded his fatwas and his legal positions (madhahib) in fiqh except Ibn Mas'ud. He would abandon his own position and view in favor of the view of Umar, and he hardly ever opposed him in any of his positions, and he would revert from his own opinion to Umar's opinion."

Al-Sha'bi said: "Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) did not perform qunut, and he said: 'If Umar had performed qunut, Abdullah would have performed qunut.'"

[Section: Uthman ibn Affan]

Uthman ibn Affan was also among those who issued fatwas. Ibn Jarir said: "However, he had no well-known companions, and those who transmitted from Umar his fatwas, his legal positions, and his rulings in the religion after him were more numerous than those who transmitted and conveyed from Uthman."

[Ali ibn Abi Talib]

As for Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him), his rulings and fatwas spread widely. But may Allah fight the Shi'a, for they corrupted much of his knowledge by lying about him. For this reason you find that the people of hadith among the authentic collectors do not rely on his narrations and fatwas except those transmitted through the People of his House and the companions of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, such as Ubaydah al-Salmani, Shurayh, Abu Wa'il, and others like them. He, may Allah be pleased with him and honor his face, used to complain about the lack of bearers of the knowledge that he had entrusted, as he said: "Indeed, here there is knowledge; if only I had found bearers for it."

(Section: The Word of Tawhid)

This is the word by which the heavens and the earth stand, the word upon which Allah originated all creation, the word upon which the religion (millah) was founded and the qiblah was set up, and for which the swords of jihad were drawn. It is the pure right of Allah upon all His servants. It is the word that protects blood, property and offspring in this abode, and that saves from the punishment of the grave and the punishment of the Fire. It is the banner which none enters Paradise except by, and the rope which none reaches Allah except by clinging to its cause. It is the word of Islam and the key to the Abode of Peace (dar al-salam). By it people are divided into wretched and happy, accepted and rejected. By it the abode of disbelief is separated from the abode of faith, and the abode of bliss is distinguished from the abode of misery and humiliation. It is the pillar that bears the obligatory duties (fard) and the sunnah.

And: "Whoever's last words are 'There is no god but Allah' enters Paradise."

The spirit (rawh) and essence (sirr) of this word is: singling out the Lord—may His praise be exalted, His names be sanctified, His name be blessed, His majesty be high, and there is no god besides Him—with love, veneration, glorification, fear and hope, and the consequences of these: trust (tawakkul), turning in repentance (inabah), desire (raghbah) and awe (rahbah). So He alone is loved; whatever else is loved, it is loved only as a follower of His love and as a means to increasing love for Him. He alone is feared, He alone is hoped in, He alone is relied upon, He alone is desired, He alone is dreaded, He alone is sworn by, He alone is looked to, He alone is turned to in repentance, He alone is obeyed in His command, He alone is sufficient, He alone is sought for help in calamities, He alone is sought for refuge, He alone is prostrated to, and He alone is slaughtered for, in His name. All of this is gathered in one phrase: that He alone is worshipped with all kinds of worship. This is the realization (tahqiq) of the testimony that there is no god but Allah. For this reason Allah has forbidden the Fire to whoever bears witness that there is no god but Allah with the true reality of testimony. And it is impossible that one who has truly realized the reality of this testimony and upheld it enters the Fire, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who are steadfast in their testimonies﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 33].

So he stands by his testimony outwardly and inwardly, in his heart and his body. Among people, some have a dead testimony, some have a sleeping one which awakens when roused, some have one lying down, and some have one closer to standing. It is in the heart like the spirit in the body: a dead spirit, a sick spirit that is closer to death, a spirit closer to life, and a healthy spirit standing by the body's interests.

In the authentic hadith from him (ﷺ):

"Indeed I know a word that no servant says at the time of death except that his soul finds rest (rawh) in it."

So the life of this spirit is by the life of this word within it. Just as the life of the body is by the existence of the spirit in it, and just as whoever dies upon this word is in Paradise enjoying it, so whoever lives by realizing it and upholding it, his spirit moves freely in the Garden of Refuge, and his life is the most pleasant life. He said:

﴿But as for he who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire—indeed, Paradise will be his refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 40-41].

So Paradise is his abode on the Day of Meeting.

(Benefit)

Some people know Allah through His generosity, bounty and beneficence; some know Him through pardon, forbearance and overlooking; some know Him through might and vengeance; some know Him through knowledge and wisdom; some know Him through might and majesty; some know Him through mercy, kindness and gentleness; some know Him through dominion and subjugation; and some know Him through answering their supplication, relieving their distress and fulfilling their needs.

The most comprehensive knowledge among these is that of one who knows Him through His speech. He knows a Lord in whom the attributes of perfection and the descriptions of majesty are gathered, transcendent above likeness, free from deficiencies and defects, possessing every beautiful name and every attribute of perfection, doing whatever He wills, above all things and with all things, able over all things, sustaining all things, commanding and forbidding, speaking with His religious and cosmic words, greater than all things and more beautiful than all things, the Most Merciful of the merciful, the Most Capable of the capable, the Most Wise of the wise. The Qur'an was sent down to make His servants know Him, and His straight path that leads to Him, and the state of those who travel after arriving at Him.

(Section)

There is nothing more beneficial for a servant than being truthful with his Lord in all his affairs, together with sincerity of resolve, so that he is truthful in his resolve and in his action.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But when the matter is resolved upon, if they had been true to Allah, it would have been better for them.﴾

So his happiness lies in sincerity of resolve and sincerity of action. Sincerity of resolve means its gathering and its firmness, and the absence of hesitation in it; rather, it should be a resolve that is not mixed with wavering or delay. When his resolve is sincere, there remains for him sincerity of action, which is exerting one's full capacity and striving diligently in it, and not falling short of it in anything outwardly or inwardly.

So the resolve of intention protects him from weakness of will and aspiration, and sincerity of action protects him from laziness and lethargy.

Whoever is truthful with Allah in all his affairs, Allah will do for him more than He does for others.

This truthfulness is a meaning that is compounded of soundness of sincerity (ikhlas) and truthfulness of reliance upon Allah (tawakkul), so the most truthful of people is the one whose sincerity and reliance are sound.

Ibn Abbas said: "He means that upon these people's hearts are locks."

Mujahid? No. The text says: And Muqatil said: "It means the sealing of the heart." It is as if the heart were like a door that is bolted shut, upon which a lock has been fastened. For if the lock is not opened, the door cannot be opened and what lies behind it cannot be reached. Likewise, if the seal and the lock are not removed from the heart, neither faith nor the Qur'an will enter it.

Consider the indefiniteness of "hearts" (qulub) and the definiteness of "locks" (aqfal) through its being added to the pronoun referring to the hearts. The indefiniteness of "hearts" includes the meaning of the hearts of those who have this attribute. Had He said, "Or upon the hearts are their locks," the hearts of others would not have been included in the sentence.

In His saying "its locks" (aqfaluha) with the definite form there is a kind of emphasis. For had He said "locks" (aqfal), the mind would have gone to what is known by this name. When He added them to the pronoun of the hearts, it became known that what is meant is what belongs to the heart as the lock belongs to the door. It is as if He meant "its locks" that are specific to it, which do not belong to anything else, and Allah knows best.

(Benefit)

Some of the Salaf said: Every servant has two eyes in his face with which he sees the affairs of this world, and two eyes in his heart with which he sees the affairs of the Hereafter.

So when Allah wills good for a servant, He opens the two eyes that are in his heart, and he sees with them the pleasure and bliss beyond measure that is promised by the One who is most truthful in speech.

And when He wills otherwise, He leaves him as he is, then recites: ﴿Or upon hearts are their locks?﴾

Even if the heart occupied with love of other than Allah, turning away from His remembrance, had no punishment except its rust, its hardness, and its being rendered idle from that for which it was created, that alone would suffice as a punishment.

Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Rawwad related from Nafi from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed these hearts rust just as iron rusts." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is their polish?" He said: "The recitation of the Qur'an."

Some of the gnostics said: Iron, when it is not used, is overtaken by rust until it corrupts it. Likewise the heart, when it is idle from the love of Allah, longing for Him, and His remembrance, is overcome by ignorance until it kills it and destroys it.

A man said to al-Hasan: "O Abu Sa'id, I complain to you of the hardness of my heart." He said: "Soften it with remembrance."

The hearts farthest from Allah are the hard heart, and its hardness is removed only by a disturbing love or an alarming fear.

(Section)

It should be known that the sealing, stamping and locking do not prevent the arrival of faith, by the One who unseals what He sealed, stamps and locked, and removes that seal, stamp and lock, and guides after misguidance, teaches after ignorance, directs after error, and opens the lock of the heart with the keys of His success which are in His hand, so that even if wretchedness and disbelief were written on a man's forehead, it would not be impossible for Him to erase them and write happiness and faith.

A reciter recited before Umar ibn al-Khattab: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an, or upon hearts are their locks?﴾ and there was a young man with him, who said: "O Allah, upon them are their locks, and their keys are in Your hand; none opens them but You." Umar recognised this for him and it increased him in his esteem.

Umar used to say in his supplication: "O Allah, if You have written me as wretched, then erase me and write me as happy, for You erase what You will and You establish."

The Lord, exalted, is the doer of what He wills; none can restrain Him. Two groups went astray here: the Qadariyya, who claimed that this is not within the Lord's power and does not fall under His action, since if it were within His power and the servant prevented it, that would contradict His generosity and kindness; and the Jabriyya, who claimed that when He decrees a decree or knows a thing, He does not change it after that nor act contrary to what He decreed and knew. Both groups restricted the One who is not restricted by anyone at all, while all His creation is under His restriction, legally and by decree.

(Section)

Know that Allah, glory be to Him, instilled in hearts the disposition to accept the truth, to submit to it, to be at peace with it, to find rest in it, and to love it; and He instilled in them aversion to falsehood and lies, recoil from them, doubt about them, and not finding rest in them. Had the natural dispositions remained as they are, they would never have preferred anything over the truth, would never have found rest except in it, would never have been at peace except with it, and would never have loved other than it. For this reason Allah, mighty and majestic, urged His servants to reflect upon the Qur'an, for whoever reflects upon it, his reflection necessarily produces in him necessary knowledge and firm certainty that it is truth and sincerity, indeed the most true of all truth and the most sincere of all sincerity, and that the one who brought it is the most truthful of Allah's creation, the most righteous, and the most complete in knowledge, action and recognition, as Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy.﴾ [al-Nisa: 82] And Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an, or upon hearts are their locks?﴾ [Muhammad: 24]

Had the locks been lifted from the hearts, the realities of the Qur'an would touch them, the lamps of faith would shine within them, and you would know by necessary knowledge, which is there like other intuitive matters, such as joy, pain, love and fear, that it is from Allah, that He spoke it in truth, and that Jibril conveyed it from Him to His messenger Muhammad. This witness in the heart is among the greatest witnesses, and with it Heraclius argued against Abu Sufyan when he said to him: "Does anyone of them turn back in disgust at his religion after entering it?" He said: "No." He said: "Likewise is faith, when its sweetness mixes with the cheerfulness of hearts; no one is disgusted with it."

(Section)

Pleasures are of three kinds: a bodily pleasure, an imaginary illusory pleasure, and an intellectual spiritual pleasure.

The bodily pleasure is the pleasure of eating, drinking and intercourse. Animals share this pleasure with man, so man's perfection does not lie in it, since the most deficient animals share it with him. Moreover, if it were perfection, the most excellent, noble and perfect of men would be those who eat, drink and copulate the most. Also, if it were perfection, the share of Allah's messengers, prophets and friends of it in this world would be more perfect than the share of their enemies. Since the matter is the opposite, it becomes clear that it is not in itself perfection, and it becomes perfection only when it includes help toward the greatest lasting pleasure, as has preceded.

As for the imaginary illusory pleasure, it is the pleasure of leadership, of exalting oneself over creation, of pride and of domineering over them.

Although those who seek this are of nobler souls than those who seek the first pleasure, its pains and the harms and corruptions it entails are greater than the soul's delight in it. Its holder is set to oppose everyone who exalts himself over him and rules over him. It has conditions and rights which cause its holder to lose much of his sensual pleasures, and it is not completed except by bearing hardships and pains greater than them. So in reality this is not a pleasure, even if the soul rejoices in it and is glad to attain it. It has been said that there is no true pleasure in this world; its end is only the removal of pain, as hunger and thirst are removed by pain-relief, and the pain of desire is removed by eating, drinking and intercourse. Likewise the pain of obscurity and loss of esteem among people is removed by leadership, rank and prestige. The verification is that pleasure is an existential matter which entails the removal of pain, by the opposition between them.

As for the intellectual spiritual pleasure, it is like the pleasure of knowledge and recognition, and of being characterized by attributes of perfection such as generosity, munificence, chastity, courage, patience, forbearance, manliness and others. The delight in these is among the greatest pleasures; it is the pleasure of the virtuous, exalted, noble soul. When the pleasure in these is joined with the pleasure of knowing Allah, exalted, loving Him, worshipping Him alone without partner, and being content with Him in place of everything, and not compensated for Him by anything else, then the holder of this pleasure is in a hastened paradise, whose relation to the pleasures of this world is like the relation of the pleasure of Paradise to the pleasure of this world. There is nothing sweeter, more delightful, more pleasant or more blissful for the heart and spirit than the love of Allah, turning to Him, worshipping Him alone, the coolness of the eye in Him, the intimacy of His nearness, and longing for His meeting and vision. The weight of a single atom of this pleasure does not equal mountains of worldly pleasures. For this reason, the weight of an atom of faith in Allah and His messenger saves one from eternal abiding in the abode of pains, so how much more so the faith that prevents entering it.

Some of the gnostics said: Whoever's eye is cooled by Allah, every eye is cooled by him; and whoever's eye is not cooled by Allah, his soul is cut to pieces over the world with sorrows. It suffices for the excellence and nobility of this pleasure that it brings forth from the heart the pain of regret over what this world loses, until one suffers from the greatest things its people delight in and flees from them as one flees from what pains.

This is a place where the judge is taste, not mere tongue of knowledge.

One of the gnostics used to say: "The poor people of this world leave the world without tasting its goodly bliss."

It is said to him: "And what is that?"

He says: "The love of Allah, intimacy with Him, longing for His meeting, and knowledge of His names and attributes."

Another said: "The best thing in this world is knowing Him and loving Him, and the sweetest thing in the Hereafter is seeing Him and hearing His speech without intermediary."

Another said: "By Allah, there pass over the heart moments in which I say: if the people of Paradise are in such a state, they are truly in a good life."

You see the love of One whose love is torment of heart and spirit, how it obliges its holder to a pleasure he wishes never to be parted from, as the poet of the Hamasa said:

"The lovers complained of passion; would that I bore alone what they suffer from among them,
So for my heart was all the pleasure of love, and no lover before me or after me has attained it."

Rabi'a said: "They occupied their hearts with love of the world away from Allah. Had they left it, the hearts would have roamed the kingdom and then returned to them with rare benefits."

Sahl al-Khawass said: "You left Him and turned to one another. Had you turned to Him, you would have seen wonders."

A woman among the worshippers said: "Had I looked into the hearts of believers with my thought, at what is stored up for them behind the veils of the unseen of the good of the Hereafter, no life in this world would have been pure for them, and no eye in this world would have been cooled for them."

Some lovers said: "His love, mighty and majestic, occupies the hearts of its lovers from delighting in the love of other than Him. So they have no pleasure in this world alongside His love that approaches His love, and they hope for no reward in the Hereafter greater in their estimation than gazing upon the face of their Beloved."

Some of the Salaf said: "There is no servant without two eyes in his face with which he sees the affairs of this world, and two eyes in his heart with which he sees the affairs of the Hereafter.

When Allah wills good for a servant, He opens the two eyes that are in his heart, and he sees with them the pleasure and bliss beyond measure that is promised by the One who is most truthful in speech.

And when He wills otherwise, He leaves him as he is, then recites: ﴿Or upon hearts are their locks?﴾"

Even if the heart occupied with love of other than Allah, turning away from His remembrance, had no punishment except its rust, its hardness, and its being rendered idle from that for which it was created, that alone would suffice as a punishment.

Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Rawwad related from Nafi from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Indeed these hearts rust just as iron rusts." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is their polish?" He said: "The recitation of the Qur'an."

Some of the gnostics said: Iron, when it is not used, is overtaken by rust until it corrupts it. Likewise the heart, when it is idle from the love of Allah, longing for Him, and His remembrance, is overcome by ignorance until it kills it and destroys it.

A man said to al-Hasan: "O Abu Sa'id, I complain to you of the hardness of my heart." He said: "Soften it with remembrance."

The hearts farthest from Allah are the hard heart, and its hardness is removed only by a disturbing love or an alarming fear.

It is said: What is the cause for which the lover delights in his love even if he does not attain his beloved?

It is said: Love produces movement of the soul and intense pursuit of it. The soul was created naturally in motion, like the movement of fire. Love is its natural movement. Whoever loves anything finds in his love pleasure and spirit. When it is empty of love entirely, the soul becomes idle from its movement, heavy, lazy, and loses the lightness of vigor. For this reason you find the lazy people the most anxious, distressed and sorrowful, with no joy or happiness. In contrast, the people of vigor and diligence in work, whatever work it is, if their vigor is in a work whose good ends and sweet outcome they know, their delight in its love and their vigor in it is stronger.

And success is from Allah.

This guarantee is only through their faith and their deeds, which are among the soldiers of Allah. He protects them by means of them, and He does not separate them from them or cut them off from them so as to nullify them for them, just as He nullifies (yatir) the deeds of the disbelievers and the hypocrites when those deeds were for other than Him and did not conform to His command.
